clue.text: Where to comfortably enjoy Spooner's schmaltzy music (4,6)

definitions.note: The definition names a place and an activity rather than a thing, which is how the setter gets a plural piece of furniture out of a 'where' phrase.

indicators.note: The Reverend Spooner traded the opening sounds of two words, so his name alone is the instruction to swap them over.

blocks.note: schmaltzy is cheesy, and airs are tunes — that is the plain pair Spooner is handed
say those two words with their opening sounds exchanged: the CH crosses over to the second word and the long E is left at the front of the first

explanation.walkthrough: The surface offers a sentimental concert; the Reverend's swap turns it into furniture. 'Airs' for tunes is the old sense that makes the plain version sound natural.
explanation.definitionFit: An easy chair is the padded armchair you sink into, so a pair of them is precisely where you would settle to enjoy something comfortably.

clue.text: Key limes regularly seen in trees (4)

indicators.note: Something done regularly happens at a fixed interval, and the interval wanted here is every second letter.

blocks.note: take every second letter across the two words, starting with the second letter of the first

explanation.walkthrough: Key limes are a real variety, small and sharp, which is what keeps the surface innocent — nothing about the fruit suggests woodland.
explanation.definitionFit: Elms are one kind of tree, so the definition names the class the answer belongs to: general standing for particular, plural for plural.

clue.text: Seven in number. Satanic? Originally (4)

definitions.note: In an &lit the definition is the whole clue, a description of the answer rather than a phrase that could be swapped in for it, so it carries no plural of its own.

indicators.note: The origin of a written word is the letter it starts with, so 'originally' asks for the opening letter of each word.

blocks.note: the initial letters of those four words, taken in the order they stand

explanation.walkthrough: Read straight, the clue describes the deadly seven and who they were traditionally blamed on; read as wordplay, each word simply hands over its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: The seven deadly sins are seven in number and were traditionally laid at Satan's door, so the whole clue reads as a plain description of them.

clue.text: Unimportant employee with no trace - bit of inkling they know (11)

definitions.note: The definition is a clause rather than a noun: 'they know' stands in for the people who know, which is what this plural answer names.

indicators.note: A bit of something is a small piece of it, and the smallest piece of a written word is the letter it opens with.

blocks.note: a cog in the machine is the standard image for a worker who counts for little
a trace is a scent, so those two words are written out as they stand
the letter INKLING opens with

explanation.walkthrough: The surface grumbles about a nobody in the office and the answer is the opposite — the people in the know. It is Italian for 'those who know'.
explanation.definitionFit: Cognoscenti are the people with expert knowledge of a subject, so the relative clause 'they know' stands exactly where the plural noun would.

clue.text: Broadcast: food's price to go up (7)

blocks.note: to air a programme is to broadcast it
fare is what is set before you to eat, as in bill of fare

explanation.walkthrough: The colon makes it read as a headline about grocery inflation, so 'price to go up' looks like a verb phrase about rising costs rather than a noun.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the price of a flight, and 'to go up' is the setter's way of saying by air rather than of anything getting dearer.

clue.text: Perform hiphop about old admiral? I'll tell you where to go (4,3)

definitions.text: I'll tell you where to go
definitions.note: The definition is spoken in the answer's own voice — a whole clause rather than a noun phrase, the object saying what it is for.

indicators.note: 'About' is positional here — placed around, the way a coat goes about your shoulders — not the 'concerning' sense the surface wants.

blocks.note: to rap is to perform hiphop, and this is the word that gets opened up
o = old, the usual abbreviation
adm. is the standard shortening of the naval rank

explanation.walkthrough: 'I'll tell you where to go' reads as the opening of an argument, which is the misdirection — it is a flat statement of what the thing does for a driver.
explanation.definitionFit: A road map tells you which way to travel, so the first-person boast is the object describing its own job.

clue.text: Talked of colours in prunes dramatically (4)

indicators.note: Talking of something is saying it out loud, so what follows is to be judged by sound rather than by spelling.

blocks.note: colours are hues, and that word said aloud can be written a second way

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a gardener attacking a shrub, and 'talked of' quietly moves the wordplay from ink to sound. Hewing is axe-work, so 'dramatically' is fair warning.
explanation.definitionFit: To hew is to chop with heavy strokes, which is pruning taken to an extreme — hence the 'dramatically' the setter attaches.

clue.text: English feasted on novel - one from 1952 (4,2,4)

indicators.note: A novel thing is a new one, so the letters are asked for in an arrangement they have not been in before — the noun sense is the surface's decoy.

blocks.note: e = English, the standard abbreviation
anagram fodder, nine letters, with the E joined on

explanation.walkthrough: 'Novel' is the trap: it looks like the definition sitting where a definition would sit, and it is the anagram signal, leaving 'one' to carry the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: East of Eden is John Steinbeck's novel of 1952, so 'one' points back at the word before it and the date says which book.

clue.text: So let baby cavort; they won't frighten the horses (6,4)

definitions.note: The definition is a clause describing the people rather than a noun naming them, and it leans on the old idiom about not frightening the horses — doing nothing that would alarm anybody.

indicators.note: To cavort is to leap about with no order to it, which is what the letters are being told to do.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, ten letters — the printed version dropped the S from 'lets' and the Observer corrected it online the same day; without that S the fodder is a letter short

explanation.walkthrough: Count the fodder before you trust it: as printed it is one letter shy, and the paper reissued the clue with 'lets' that Sunday. The horses are the giveaway.
explanation.definitionFit: Stable boys spend their days among horses, so the horses are used to them — the clue defines the job by the calm it leaves behind.

clue.text: Concerning boss's hidey-hole, say, an American in retirement (10)

indicators.note: Someone in retirement has withdrawn from the field, and a withdrawing across entry is read the other way — right to left along the row.

blocks.note: a lair is an animal's hidey-hole
eg = say, in the sense 'for example'
the article taken at face value
am. is the standard shortening of American

explanation.walkthrough: Everything is assembled forwards and then read backwards, so the clue runs left to right while the entry is built right to left. 'Say' = EG is worth keeping; it turns up constantly.
explanation.definitionFit: Managerial means having to do with a manager, and boss is the everyday word for one, so the adjective sits straight over 'concerning'.

clue.text: Perhaps ChatGPT's a step back for most of humanity (4)

indicators.note: Stepping back takes you the way you came, so the letters are read in the opposite direction — right to left across the row.

blocks.note: ChatGPT is one instance of AI — 'perhaps' flags the example — and the 's brings an S with it
the article at face value

explanation.walkthrough: The surface argues that machines are a backward step for us all, and the answer is a continent. Modern crossword shorthand: a named chatbot is there to give you AI.
explanation.definitionFit: Asia holds around sixty per cent of the world's people, so the setter names the continent by the share of humanity living in it.

clue.text: Dodgy moolah for nun: forgive the transgression (2,4,2,4)

definitions.note: The answer is a set phrase, not a verb: it is what you say in order to forgive a transgression, so the definition describes the job the phrase does.

indicators.note: Dodgy means not to be trusted, and letters that cannot be trusted will not stay in the order the clue gives them.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, twelve letters — moolah is slang for money

explanation.walkthrough: 'Dodgy moolah for nun' paints a small scandal and the phrase that comes out waves the whole thing away, which is the joke of the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the American basketball phrase for a foul that cost nobody anything, said to wave a transgression away instead of punishing it.

clue.text: Creation on the fringes: bizarrely, it's our trade (8,3)

indicators.note: Something done bizarrely is done in a strange, unexpected way, and letters handled like that come out in a strange order.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, eleven letters

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a couple of craftspeople describing their line of work, and the answer is what galleries call art made right outside the art world.
explanation.definitionFit: Outsider art is work by self-taught makers beyond the mainstream, so the phrase names both the making and the position it is made from.

clue.text: One signing in and restarting after revision (10)

indicators.note: A revision is a reworking, so the word comes back with its letters worked over into another arrangement.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, ten letters

explanation.walkthrough: 'Signing in' and 'restarting' both belong to the same computer screen, which is what makes the definition so hard to see as a definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A registrant is somebody who has put their name on a register, which is exactly what signing in amounts to.

clue.text: May, say, but may ... not (6,4)

blocks.note: with its capital, May is a month and a surname — a name for one particular thing, which is the test being applied
in lower case the same three letters are an ordinary verb of permission, no kind of name, and so fail that test

explanation.walkthrough: One word inspected twice. A capital at the start of a clue is invisible, since every clue starts with one, which is why 'May, say' looks like an example of something else.
explanation.definitionFit: A proper noun is a name for a particular person, place or month, so capital-M May qualifies while the modal verb never could.

clue.text: What makes a lug smart? (7)

blocks.note: lug is northern and Scottish slang for the thing you hear with
to smart is to sting or hurt — the verb, not the adjective the surface suggests

explanation.walkthrough: Read as a question it is a riddle, read as instructions it is two words laid end to end, and both readings land on the same thing. That double duty is what &lit means.
explanation.definitionFit: The whole clue reads straight: the complaint named is precisely a pain in the ear, so the question doubles as its own definition.

clue.text: Swap other basket - that contains culinary flavouring (3-4)

indicators.note: Something that contains a thing has it inside, and the containing here is literal — the letters are sitting inside the words themselves.

blocks.note: the letters run on consecutively from the end of the first word, straight through the second and into the start of the third

explanation.walkthrough: 'Swap' invites you to rearrange the letters of what follows, and that is the trap: nothing moves here, and the whole answer has been lying in plain sight all along.
explanation.definitionFit: A pot-herb is any leaf grown for the cooking pot — parsley, sorrel, chervil — so it is a flavouring in the kitchen sense.

clue.text: Everyman's to send text: Everyman's beginning to intrude (7)

indicators.note: The beginning of a written word is the letter it starts with, so only that single opening letter is wanted.

blocks.note: Everyman is what this setter calls himself, so 'Everyman's' is I'M
to ping somebody is to send them a quick message
the letter the setter's name starts with

explanation.walkthrough: Everyman signs his own clues, so his name means both I'M and the letter it opens with — the same word doing two different jobs a few syllables apart.
explanation.definitionFit: To impinge on something is to encroach on it, which is what intruding is: advancing into a place you were not invited.

clue.text: Sap getting a kind of pipe (7)

blocks.note: the verb sense: to sap somebody is to drain their strength away
a noun and a different word altogether — the tube that carries burnt gases out of an engine

explanation.walkthrough: The two senses share a spelling and nothing else, and 'getting' is there only to join them. 'A kind of' is the usual flag that a category, not a synonym, is being pointed at.
explanation.definitionFit: To exhaust somebody is to sap their energy, and an exhaust is the pipe venting an engine's spent gases: one verb, one noun.

clue.text: Abrupt notion: run into intelligence agent like Black Widow? (7)

indicators.note: An abrupt ending stops before it should, so the word is cut short of its final letter.
'Into' puts one thing inside another, so what stands before it is buried in what comes after.

blocks.note: a spy is an intelligence agent, and it is this word that gets opened up
a notion is an IDEA, docked of its last letter
r = run, the cricket scorer's abbreviation

explanation.walkthrough: Black Widow is the Marvel spy, which is why the definition sits so quietly at the end. The clue wants the other black widow, the one with eight legs.
explanation.definitionFit: The answer means like a spider, and a black widow is a spider — the question mark marks a definition by example rather than a synonym.

clue.text: Small bed with couple and pooch (7)

blocks.note: s = small, as on a clothing label
a cot is a small bed
to couple two things is to tie them together — the verb, not the pair

explanation.walkthrough: A nationality falls out of the first two pieces by accident, which is half the pleasure: 'small bed' has nothing to do with Scotland and produces it anyway.
explanation.definitionFit: A Scottie is a Scottish terrier and pooch is affectionate slang for a dog, so the general word is defining one particular breed.

clue.text: What gets wetter when it dries up in Istanbul? (7,5)

definitions.text: What gets wetter when it dries up in Istanbul?

blocks.clueFragment: What gets wetter when it dries
blocks.note: the old riddle: whatever does the drying takes on all the water it removes, so it ends up soaked
'dries up' looks like one phrase about a drought; split it and the rest is only saying which country the thing comes from

explanation.walkthrough: The paradox is literally true rather than a trick of words, and Istanbul is there to supply the nationality — the plain word on its own would be four letters short.
explanation.definitionFit: A Turkish towel is the thick looped-cotton bath towel, and a towel is the answer to the old riddle about growing wetter as it dries.

clue.text: A friendly 'hello' in Naples - or quite the opposite (4)

blocks.note: Naples is doing no more than telling you which language to greet somebody in
the very same word is what Italians say on leaving, so the greeting doubles as a farewell

explanation.walkthrough: One word for both ends of a meeting is unusual in English, which is why the clue can define it twice and still read as a single sentence about Italy.
explanation.definitionFit: Ciao is the Italian greeting used both on arrival and on departure, so 'hello' and its opposite are equally accurate.

clue.text: Maybe Blyton's a bit uneven? I daresay (4)

indicators.note: A bit of something is a small piece taken from inside it, which is exactly where these letters are sitting.

blocks.note: the letters run on from the end of the first word, through the one-letter word, and into the start of the last

explanation.walkthrough: 'A bit uneven' reads as mild criticism of the writing, which is the innocent surface a hidden word needs, and the capital I helps disguise the join.
explanation.definitionFit: It was Blyton's first name, so the definition points at the answer through the surname everyone knows — 'maybe' flags one example among many.

clue.text: Tiny thing seen in first half of dictionary (4)

blocks.note: a dictionary runs from A to Z, so the half you reach first stops at M, and that span written out as a range is the wordplay

explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay takes no letters out of the word 'dictionary' at all — it is the range the entries cover, written as you would say it.
explanation.definitionFit: An atom is the smallest unit of an element, the everyday byword for something too small to see.

clue.text: Gold pin Arthur's taken back - is he from Perth? (10)

indicators.note: Taking something back sends it the way it came, so those letters are read from the right-hand end of the row instead.

blocks.note: au is the chemical symbol for gold, from the Latin aurum
a nail is a pin you hammer in
Art is the familiar short form of Arthur, and the 's comes along with it

explanation.walkthrough: Perth is the trap — there is one in Scotland too, and an Arthur nudges you towards it. The reversal runs across both of the last two pieces at once, not just the pin.
explanation.definitionFit: Perth is the state capital of Western Australia, so a man from there is one — a definition by a single city standing for the whole country.

clue.text: Cistern to fail - at great cost (4)

blocks.note: the plain noun: a large container for holding water
the verb, borrowed from American sport and the box office, where a film that flops expensively is said to do this

explanation.walkthrough: A dash is all that separates the two definitions, which is why the clue reads as one sentence about a plumbing disaster.
explanation.definitionFit: The noun is a cistern for storing water and the verb is to fail spectacularly, usually of a film losing money — same spelling, unrelated senses.

clue.text: Trendy dining option: Coronation chicken? (6,4)

blocks.note: Coronation Street is Britain's longest-running television soap, so the name supplies the word that follows it
chicken is one example of the general category, so the category is what the word gives you

explanation.walkthrough: Coronation chicken is a real dish, invented for the Queen's coronation in 1953, and that is the whole misdirection: those two words belong to different halves of the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: It is what is cooked and sold from stalls and vans, the fashionable way of eating out that the definition is pointing at.
